projectSummary: The trial supports the statement that eight weeks of low-load bench press training increases pectoralis major thickness in untrained young men, and reports no detectable difference against a push-up. The identical printed pectoralis values make the between-group pectoralis comparison unusable as a numeric estimate; the within-group direction is still legible because both arms increased.

publication.statusSource: Crossref REST API works record plus the Crossref/Retraction Watch CSV export, both fetched 2026-09-13

notes: The duplicated pectoralis major values are a data-integrity problem that the published text does not explain.
Nine participants per arm gives very low power to detect a between-group difference, and the report treats absence of a significant difference as similarity.
Post-testing at 48 hours after the last session leaves acute swelling as a plausible contaminant of a tier-1 measurement.
A protein supplement was given to both arms, which is balanced but changes the intervention from exercise alone.
Load was fixed at 40 per cent 1RM, far below the loads usually prescribed for hypertrophy.

study.intervention: bench press at 40 per cent 1RM; push-up with position adjusted to the same load
study.population: Eighteen male participants, age 20.2 (SD 0.73) years, range 19-22, height 169.8 (SD 4.4) cm, weight 64.5 (SD 4.7) kg, were randomly assigned to bench press at 40 per cent 1RM (n = 9) or push-up adjusted to the same load (n = 9), twice per week for eight weeks, performed to failure with 2-min rest intervals.

title: Low-load bench press and push-up induce similar muscle hypertrophy and strength gain.
